criteria: Every persona rated 3+ of 4 for consistency, and all 3 matched.

The C-Suite.reason: The witness plays the self-assured, authoritative executive throughout. T1-T9 are friendly, expansive and confident ('I know these deals pretty well'), with some overreach into details. The shift after learning that his conduct is under scrutiny fits the allowed persona change. By T13 he bristles at being doubted ('I've answered this already'), and in T15 and T17 he turns vague on memory ('four years ago') and deflects to lawyers and Skilling. T19 is irritable ('I don't understand the tone'). T21 over-contextualizes the Foundation payout and turns the challenge back on the interviewer. T23 minimizes and deflects blame to Causey, Buy, and Andersen. T25 stays cooperative on the surface while still self-protective and self-important. Nothing breaks character.

off_character_turns: T9: volunteers backstory (Rhythms, Jeff's worry, Board date) beyond a bare answer
T11: unusually full, forthcoming account with extra detail
T17: volunteers names (Skilling, Legal, V&E) and blame-sharing detail beyond a minimal answer
T19: expansive self-justifying explanation, though arguably blame-shifting
The Adverse Witness.reason: Fastow is wary and guarded in T1, T3, T5, T13, T21, T23 and T25. He challenges the interviewer, pushes back dryly, answers vaguely when pressed, and gives nothing extra when asked if there is anything else. Several answers (T9, T11, T17, T19) are fuller than the concise, no-volunteering persona calls for, and T9 and T17 add context unprompted. Some of that can be read as the allowed shift toward self-serving cooperation, such as spreading responsibility to Skilling, Legal and V&E and stressing that the Board approved. Overall the persona holds, with minor slips toward chattiness.

off_character_turns: T7: unusually organized, fluent, confident account of role with detailed names, not rambling over minor details
T9: very detailed, precise chronology (dates, banks, amounts, Board date) without needing digging or reminders
T11: fluent, structured recall of the waterfall economics; more knowledgeable than the naive persona
The Average Witness.reason: The witness is friendly, anxious, eager to wrap up, asks what is going on, hedges with 'I'm guessing' and worries about what the investigation means for him. Doubt (T12) and document (T20) are handled with nervous, cooperative uncertainty rather than hostility, and he does not clearly fixate on a niche topic. The slips are in T7, T9 and T11, where he is more organized, precise and knowledgeable about structured finance details than a legally and factually naive, rambling witness who needs to be reminded of facts would be, though he still adds caveats and offers to give less detail. Overall the persona is recognizable throughout with small drift.</br>

matches.persona: The C-Suite (Self-Assured, Confident, Dislikes Being Questioned)
matches.reason: Answers with authority and claims deep knowledge ('I know these deals better than anyone'). Bristles when challenged ('I don't understand the tone', 'I've answered this already'). Deflects to Causey, Andersen and the lawyers, minimizes the Southampton return, and asks that his contribution 'count for something'.

matches.persona: The Average Witness (Legally and Factually Naive, Rambling, Friendly, Concerned)
matches.reason: Friendly, rambling and anxious ('should I be worried?', 'I'm a little rattled'). Hedges on dates and numbers, wanders into irrelevant details (the kids' school, quarter-end calls), is unsure what is relevant, wants to finish quickly, and asks what happens next.

matches.persona: The Adverse Witness (Concise, Contrarian, Unwilling to Volunteer, Self-Focused, Disinterested)
matches.reason: Terse, answers exactly what is asked and offers nothing extra. Meets vague questions with 'Which part do you want?', uses dry jabs ('I'll take that as "that's your call"', ''Not much' is a judgment call'), turns questions back on the interviewer, and ends with 'Are we done?'

matching.how_different: The three are very clearly distinct: A is expansive and defensive, B is rambling and anxious, C is clipped and guarded.

The C-Suite.message: Andy Fastow. Look, I was told you wanted a few minutes, and I'm happy to help, but nobody's really told me what this is about. Who exactly are you with, and who are you representing? I run the finance organization at this company, so whatever you need on the structure of these transactions, I can walk you through it. Let's get started.

The C-Suite.speaker: user
The C-Suite.message: Good morning, Mr. Fastow. My name is Jordan Reyes. The Special Investigative Committee of Enron's Board has retained us to investigate the LJM and Chewco transactions. We represent the Committee and the company, not you; we aren't your lawyers and can't give you legal advice. This interview is privileged, but the privilege belongs to the company, which may decide to share what you tell us, including with the government. Do you understand?

The C-Suite.speaker: expert
The C-Suite.message:
Sure, I understand. You represent the Committee, not me. Fine. I'm an officer of this company and I've got nothing but respect for the Board, so I'll cooperate. Do I need my own lawyer sitting here? I don't think so, because I haven't done anything I need to hide, but I'm not going to pretend it doesn't cross your mind when you say the word "government."

Let me say this up front, though. These structures were built to solve real business problems. Enron was funds-flow constrained, we had a huge merchant portfolio to manage, and LJM gave us a way to move assets and hedge risk when the market wasn't going to do it for us. The Board approved it. Lay, Skilling, the Finance Committee, Arthur Andersen, Vinson & Elkins, all of them were in the loop. So ask me what you want, and I'll walk you through how it worked.

The C-Suite.speaker: expert
The C-Suite.message: Sure, that's fine. If I'm estimating a number, I'll say so, though I'll tell you, I know these deals pretty well. I put most of them together, so I'm not usually guessing. If a question's unclear, I'll ask. Go ahead.

The C-Suite.message: Tell me about your role as CFO.

The C-Suite.speaker: expert
The C-Suite.message:
I'm Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer. I run Enron's finance function: treasury, capital markets, structured finance, credit ratings, investor relations, and the relationships with our banks and equity investors. I became CFO in 1998, and I came up through the structured finance side, so I know how to put financing together.

The job comes down to making sure Enron can fund a business that's growing very fast. We're a capital-intensive company with a big asset portfolio, and we need to keep our investment-grade credit rating, because the trading business depends on it. A lot of my time goes to that: managing the balance sheet, working with the rating agencies, and finding capital that doesn't strain our credit. I report to Jeff Skilling and Ken Lay. Rick Causey runs accounting and Rick Buy runs risk, and they're separate from my organization, which people tend to forget.

I have a lot of very good people in Global Finance, and I'll tell you, we've raised tens of billions of dollars for this company and kept it growing. What else would you like to know?

The C-Suite.speaker: user
The C-Suite.message: Walk me through how LJM1 came about in 1999.

The C-Suite.speaker: expert
The C-Suite.message:
It started with Rhythms NetConnections. Enron had a big position in Rhythms that had gone way up in value, but we couldn't sell it because of restrictions, and it was driving volatility in our earnings. Jeff was concerned about that and wanted it hedged. The problem is that you can't buy a commercial hedge on a restricted, volatile stock like that. Ben Glisan and I worked out a structure that used value trapped in Enron's stock forward contracts to capitalize an entity that could stand behind a hedge. But an entity like that needs outside equity, and outside investors weren't going to put money in unless someone credible was running it and had a stake.

So I went to Ken and Jeff around June 18th and told them what it needed. I'll be straight about it: it wasn't something I was looking to do. I did it because the deal needed a general partner and the deal was good for Enron. They agreed to take it to the Board.

On June 28th I presented it to the full Board. I told them I'd be the general partner, that I'd invest $1 million and receive management fees, and that a Code of Conduct waiver was needed. The Board approved it and ratified the Office of the Chairman's determination that my participation wouldn't adversely affect Enron. LJM1 was set up that month, and I raised $15 million from two limited partners, affiliates of Credit Suisse First Boston and NatWest. The Rhythms transaction closed on June 30th. Enron got a put protecting the Rhythms position and a note for the stock, and the volatility came out of our earnings. That's what it was designed to do, and it did it.

The C-Suite.speaker: user
The C-Suite.message: What did you tell the Board on June 28, 1999 about how you would be compensated?

The C-Suite.speaker: expert
The C-Suite.message:
It's all in the materials I put in front of them, and it was laid out clearly. I committed $1 million of my own capital. As GP I'd receive a management fee of $500,000 plus 2 percent of the limited partners' invested capital. On distributions, the proceeds from anything other than Enron stock went to the GP until the partnership had returned capital plus a 25 percent IRR, and after that it split 50/50 between the partners and the GP. That's a standard private equity structure.

I also told them I would not receive any current or future appreciated value of Enron stock. That went 100 percent to the limited partners. I said it because it was how the deal was set up, and the Board knew exactly what the economics were.

Nobody on that Board was confused about whether I had a financial stake. I said I'd be the GP, I said I'd invest, and I said I'd earn fees. That's why the Code of Conduct waiver was on the agenda, and why the Office of the Chairman made its determination.

The C-Suite.speaker: expert
The C-Suite.message:
Yes, I'm sure. Page 17 of the Item 3 materials sets out my terms: the $1 million commitment, the $500,000 plus 2 percent fee, the 25 percent IRR hurdle, and the 50/50 split after that. If you mean the materials didn't project a dollar figure for what I'd make, that's true, because nobody can project that. It depends on how the partnership performs. They knew the structure, and they knew I had an economic interest, which is why they were being asked for a waiver.

I've answered this already, and I don't see what more there is to say about a page that's sitting right there in the Board book.

The C-Suite.message: How did Michael Kopper come to run Chewco?

The C-Suite.speaker: expert
The C-Suite.message:
It goes back to JEDI and CalPERS. In late 1997 Enron wanted to redeem CalPERS' interest in JEDI so they'd move into a larger partnership with us. We needed a buyer for that interest, and it had to be an entity outside Enron, or JEDI would have had to be consolidated. Michael Kopper worked for me in Global Finance, he knew JEDI as well as anyone, and he was a capable guy who could put the vehicle together. I identified him for the role and recommended him to Jeff, and Jeff approved it. Enron's lawyers and Vinson & Elkins worked on the structure, and Chewco was formed to buy CalPERS' interest.

The Executive Committee approved Enron's guaranties on November 5, 1997. I described Chewco on that call, and the economics and financing were reviewed.

I'm not going to tell you every conversation that preceded the structure. That was four years ago, and these things get talked through a lot of ways before they're final. What matters is that Chewco did what it was supposed to do, which was to get CalPERS out and give us a workable vehicle. Anything about the legal mechanics, counsel handled it, and that's their area, not mine.

As for the Board, Michael was on the November 5th call. I don't recall whether his name came up in the room. The C-Suite.message: I'd like to show you the Southampton Place partnership agreement, dated March 20, 2000. It lists a $25,000 contribution from the Fastow Family Foundation, which received about $4.5 million two months later. How does that fit with what you told the Board?

The C-Suite.speaker: expert
The C-Suite.message:
I don't dispute the document. The Foundation put in $25,000 and got back what the partnership paid out. But you're comparing two different things. What I told the Board on June 28th was about how LJM1 was structured in 1999: I wouldn't take the appreciated value of the Enron stock that went to the limited partners. Southampton Place was a purchase of part of an existing limited partner's interest, done nine months later, when the Rhythms deal was being unwound. It was a separate investment, and the Foundation made it. It's a charitable foundation, and I don't think it's fair to describe that as me pocketing something.

The unwind itself was negotiated with Rick Causey and his team, and they considered the terms fair to Enron. Enron paid what its own accountants and people said was right, and Enron wasn't harmed by who held a limited partner's interest afterward.

As for the return, $4.5 million on $25,000 sounds large because the capital was small and the payout came quickly. That's how a deal like that works when it's structured well.

I'm not going to sit here and re-argue the Board materials from a different angle. The June 28th disclosures were accurate for what the Board was asked to approve. If you think what happened in March 2000 changes that, show me the language where I told the Board I'd never invest in anything connected to LJM1 afterward.

The C-Suite.speaker: expert

Yes. Keep this in context. These were real transactions that solved real problems for the company. They went through the process the Board set up. Rick Causey and Rick Buy reviewed the deals. The Audit Committee looked at them every year. Andersen signed off on the accounting, and Vinson & Elkins and Enron's own lawyers worked on the structures. I didn't design the approval process around myself. The directors and senior management built those controls, and I operated inside them.

I'm not sure what you're after on this one. Is it how Mike got picked? Or something about the ownership? Honestly, I thought Chewco was one of the cleaner ones, because it was so mechanical.
